summary:
Portugal remains one of the safer destinations in Europe for transgender visitors. Homosexuality is legal, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, gender-affirming care is available, legal gender and name change is possible without restriction under the 2018 self-determination law, self-declaration is available from age 16, bathroom access matching a person's gender is protected, discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is illegal, conversion therapy has been banned since 2024, and surgical intervention on intersex infants is prohibited.

The Penal Code treats sexual orientation and gender identity as explicit grounds for aggravated offences. Under Articles 132, 144 and 145, an assault determined by hatred on those grounds is aggravated and punishable by up to four years, and organising discrimination on those grounds carries penalties of one to eight years.

That baseline is under direct legislative pressure. On 20 March 2026 the Assembly of the Republic approved on first reading three bills tabled by the governing PSD, the far-right Chega and the CDS-PP, by 124 votes to 79. The package targets the 2018 self-identification law directly. One bill would reinstate a mandatory medical opinion for any change of legal gender and name, undoing the reform that replaced medical certification with self-declaration. The bills were referred to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees.

The rollback package also threatens the statutory ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children, according to ILGA-Europe's assessment of the draft legislation. Committee-stage analysis by the Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality warns that the bills worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people, and defends the existing discrimination-prevention duties of schools.

As of the most recent reporting none of the three bills has become law. The measures sit at committee stage after a first vote, and the Justice Ministry continues to process legal gender and name changes under the 2018 framework.

The ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map 2026 places Portugal 12th, down one position, with a score of 67 percent. The rating reflects the absence of any new affirmative legislation since the 2024 ban on conversion practices, and the draft bill threatening self-determined legal gender recognition and the intersex intervention ban. Portugal scores below Malta, Iceland and Belgium and above most other European states.
tangentialFactors:
The political contest over the bills has been unusually public. The psychologists' professional order and trans rights organisations describe the package as a retrocesso, a backwards step, and the socialist opposition invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta, a trans woman killed by youths in Porto, against the rollback, drawing a protest response from Chega's Hugo Soares.

Six European LGBTI organisations, IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal, issued a joint statement warning that the three bills debated on 19 March and voted on 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans and intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition. They calculate that adoption would cost Portugal at least four places on the Rainbow Map, dropping it below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France, and reversing its position as a European reference point.

The rollback has reached European-level scrutiny. A European Parliament written question, E-001183/2026, formally asks the Commission about the repeal process for the 2018 gender self-determination law and its consequences for the health and safety of transgender people in the country.

Public opinion runs against the legislative direction. Equaldex records high public support for same-sex parenting, ranked first among 30 European peer jurisdictions, while the same source records gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, a full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and protected bathroom access.

The Ombudsman, Provedoria da Justiça, has requested constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C, which criminalises acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. The institutional watchdog is questioning the hate-speech provision itself rather than expanding it, a challenge running alongside rather than against the rollback bills.
localsOnly:
Justice Ministry data show legal sex and name changes climbing back toward the high-water mark recorded two years earlier, with the largest number recorded in the capital district, according to Expresso. The uptick occurred before any tightening takes effect, so residents are completing changes under the existing self-declaration route while it remains in force.

The Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality assessed the bills in committee and concluded that they worsen suffering and adverse outcomes for trans people. The same analysis defended the discrimination-prevention duties already imposed on schools, and found the Bloco de Esquerda bill on the subject compatible with those human-rights obligations.

Residents benefit from protections that remain in force regardless of the bills: the 2018 self-determination route to legal recognition, the 2024 conversion-therapy ban, the prohibition on intersex infant surgery, aggravated-offence penalties for hatred-motivated crime, and the Ombudsman's standing to bring constitutional challenges against Penal Code provisions.

Constitutional review of Article 176-C is a domestic institutional process available to residents through the Ombudsman, distinct from the parliamentary rollback and from European-level questions raised by MEPs.
outOfScopeNotes:
The three bills are at first reading and committee stage. Their final content, the committee's report, the second reading and any presidential or constitutional review are unresolved, and reporting does not establish whether the mandatory medical opinion, the changes to the intersex provision, or any restriction on hormone treatment for minors will survive in enacted form.

The precise division of measures across the three separate bills is not consistently specified across sources. The mandatory medical opinion is attributed to the package; a ban on hormone treatment for minors is described for one of the bills in political reporting but is not separately confirmed by the committee or rights-group documents cited here.

The Rainbow Map 2026 score of 67 percent and the 12th-place ranking predate any adoption of the rollback, and the projected loss of at least four places is a projection by signatory organisations rather than a published score. Whether the rating will be revised after the legislative process concludes is unresolved.

The outcome of the Ombudsman's request for constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C is not stated in the source material, and no ruling on the provision's compatibility with the constitution is available here.

The European Parliament written question E-001183/2026 records an inquiry to the Commission; no Commission reply or any binding effect on the national legislative process is documented in the inventory.
